course.title: NumPy Mastery
course.subtitle: Complete Numerical Computing Program
course.tagline: Learn NumPy. Master Arrays. Build Data Science Skills.
course.description: NumPy from the first array to linear algebra, broadcasting, memory layout, random simulation and real Data Science workflows. Hinglish explanations, runnable code and ten practice sections per module.
prerequisites: Basic arithmetic and an idea of what a matrix is
outcomes: Create and inspect ndarrays and reason about shape, size, ndim and dtype
Index, slice, reshape and broadcast arrays without Python loops
Use universal functions, aggregation and Boolean masks correctly
Tell a view from a copy and control memory usage
Generate reproducible random data and run Monte Carlo simulations
Solve linear systems and choose stable linear-algebra routines
Read and write numeric data with NPY/NPZ and text files
Handle NaN, infinity and masked arrays in real datasets
Vectorise code and benchmark it honestly
Move arrays between NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib and scikit-learn

modules.title: NumPy Introduction and Fundamentals
modules.goal: Understand what NumPy is, why ndarrays beat Python lists for numeric work, and run your first array program.

topics.title: Create your first array
topics.body: np.array turns a Python list into an ndarray: one typed block of memory that supports vectorised maths, so mean() and shape are properties of the data rather than a loop you write.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(a, a.mean(), a.shape)

topics.title: Vectorised arithmetic
topics.body: An operation between an array and a scalar is applied to every element by compiled code, which is why `a * 2` needs no loop and returns a new array instead of mutating `a`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a * 2)

topics.title: Typed memory, not a Python list
topics.body: Every ndarray has one dtype and a fixed itemsize, so nbytes tells you the real memory it occupies; a Python list stores pointers to separate objects and cannot answer that question.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a.dtype, a.itemsize, a.nbytes)

modules.title: ndarray Fundamentals
modules.goal: Read an array's shape, size, ndim, dtype and axes correctly before writing any operation on it.

topics.title: shape, size and ndim
topics.body: shape is one number per axis, size is the product of those numbers and ndim is how many axes exist — the three answers every shape error is really about.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a.shape, a.size, a.ndim)

topics.title: dtype and itemsize
topics.body: The dtype decides how the bytes are interpreted and itemsize is the bytes per element; together they explain both the values you get and the memory you pay.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a.dtype, a.itemsize)

topics.title: Axis means the direction that is collapsed
topics.body: Reducing along axis 0 collapses rows (one result per column) and axis 1 collapses columns (one result per row); reading the output length tells you which axis was reduced.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.sum(axis=0), a.sum(axis=1))

modules.title: Array Creation and Initialization
modules.goal: Create arrays with zeros, ones, full, arange, linspace, eye and diag, and pick the right constructor for a dataset.

topics.title: zeros, ones and full
topics.body: These allocate a new array of a given shape and fill it: zeros and ones are the common starting points, full repeats any value and needs the fill value explicitly.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.zeros(3), np.ones((2, 2)), np.full(3, 7))

topics.title: arange and linspace
topics.body: arange builds a range by step (the stop is excluded, like range) while linspace builds a fixed number of evenly spaced points including both ends — the safer choice for float grids.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 10, 2), np.linspace(0, 1, 3))

topics.title: Identity and diagonal matrices
topics.body: eye builds an identity matrix of any shape and diag builds a square matrix from a 1-D vector (or extracts the diagonal from a 2-D one).
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.eye(2), np.diag([1, 2]))

modules.title: Slicing and Array Views
modules.goal: Slice arrays with start/stop/step, slice rows and columns, and know when a slice shares memory.

topics.title: Slice with a step
topics.body: A slice is start:stop:step and the stop is excluded; a step of 2 skips every other element, which is the fast way to downsample a series.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print(a[2:8:2])

topics.title: Slice rows and columns
topics.body: In 2-D the first slice selects rows and the second columns; `1:` keeps every column from index 1 onward.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[:2, 1:])

topics.title: A slice is a view
topics.body: Basic slicing returns a view, so writing into the slice writes into the original array — the most common source of "my data changed by itself".
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a[1:3]
b[0] = 99
print(a)

topics.title: ravel and transpose
topics.body: ravel flattens to one dimension (often as a view) and .T swaps rows with columns; together they move a matrix between the two layouts most libraries expect.
topics.code:

topics.title: concatenate and stack

print(np.concatenate([a, a]), np.stack([a, a]).shape)

topics.title: view shares, copy does not
topics.body: a.view() shares the same buffer so a write through the view changes the original; a.copy() allocates new memory and leaves the original alone.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
v = a.view()
c = a.copy()
v[0] = 9
print(a, c)

topics.title: Prove sharing with shares_memory
topics.body: Slicing usually returns a view, but an explicit copy never shares; shares_memory answers the question with a real check instead of a guess.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(np.shares_memory(a, a[1:3]), np.shares_memory(a, a.copy()))

topics.title: Strides describe memory steps
topics.body: strides are the bytes to move per axis; a (2, 3) int64 array steps 24 bytes per row and 8 bytes per column, which is why layout affects speed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.strides)

print(np.load('/tmp/a.npy'))

topics.title: Text and CSV round-trip
topics.body: savetxt writes human-readable numbers and loadtxt parses them back as floats, which is the portable option when another tool must read the file.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
np.savetxt('/tmp/a.txt', np.array([1, 2]))
print(np.loadtxt('/tmp/a.txt'))

topics.title: Several arrays in one NPZ
topics.body: savez stores named arrays in a single compressed-free archive and load returns a mapping whose keys are the names you gave.
topics.code:

np.savez('/tmp/a.npz', x=np.arange(2))
print(list(np.load('/tmp/a.npz').keys()))

modules.goal: Detect and handle NaN and infinity honestly, and choose masked arrays or nan-aware functions deliberately.

topics.title: NaN is not equal to anything
topics.body: isnan locates missing values and nanmean ignores them; plain mean propagates NaN, so one missing reading can hide the whole summary.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(np.isnan(a), np.nanmean(a))

topics.title: Infinity is a value, not a missing one
topics.body: isinf finds overflow and division-by-zero results; infinity is a real float value, so it must be filtered or clipped rather than treated as missing.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.isinf(np.array([1.0, np.inf])))

topics.title: Masked arrays carry their own mask
topics.body: A masked array stores a boolean mask beside the data, and reductions ignore masked positions — cleaner than overwriting values with NaN.
topics.code:
import numpy.ma as ma
a = ma.masked_array([1, 2, 3], mask=[0, 1, 0])
print(a.mean())

modules.title: Performance and Vectorization
modules.goal: Replace Python loops with vectorised code, reuse buffers with out= and benchmark changes honestly.

topics.title: Vectorised reduction
topics.body: One NumPy expression runs in compiled loops over contiguous memory, so a million-element sum needs no Python iteration.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(1_000_000)
print(int((a * 2).sum()))

topics.title: Reuse a buffer with out=
topics.body: Passing out= writes the result into an existing array, avoiding a new allocation in hot loops where the shape is already known.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
